newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso woos mayors with loans talk.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso woos mayors with loans talk.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, seeking to reduce opposition from mayors to a controversial Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF), said Tuesday they stood to receive up to $3.0 billion in international loans.
"More than half the loans from the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) are destined for municipalities," Cardoso said during a ceremony in the presidential palace.
Government officials have been talking about the IADB's program to loan Brazil up to $6.0 billion in what is seen as an attempt to win support for a bill extending the FEF until 1999.
But Planning Minister Antonio Kandir poured cold water on the president's words, saying just $600 million of the total loan package would be used by municipalities.

The FEF extension bill has been delayed several weeks amid haggling between the government's economic team and representatives of more than 5,000 mayors across Brazil who complain they will lose out from extension of the fund.

Government whips plan to put the bill to a first vote in the Chamber of Deputies later Tuesday or Wednesday. As a constitutional amendment, it needs two three-fifths majorities in each house of Congress.
The FEF allows the federal government to hold on to 20 percent of receipts earmarked by the constitution for spending by states and municipalities, plus the tax receipts of federal workers.
That adds up to about $26 billion a year which is used to plug holes in the federal budget before the remainder is passed on to local authorities.

The fund was introduced as an emergency measure in 1994, shortly after the launch of Brazil's real currency. Since then, in the absence of structural reform, it has proved itself as a key fiscal tool.

However, with the 1998 elections looming, and mayors revelling in their power to make or break the campaigns of federal lawmakers, the government faces a battle to get the two three-fifths majorities in the lower house to extend the FEF.
